commits.author: karansag
commits.message:
[iris] Require the native wheel that maps IAP user roles (#10243)

Pin marin-iris-native to 0.1.13.dev38952644761 or newer. That wheel was
built from the merge of #10070, which taught the Rust native proxy to
map a
verified IAP email through auth.user_roles before the admin list. The
lock
still pointed at the 2026-10-09 wheel, so any branch that does not touch
lib/iris/rust installs a proxy that ignores user_roles and
test_iap_principal_resolution_enforces_personal_batch_access fails with
role 'admin' instead of 'user'. Branches that change Rust build the
extension from source and pass, which is why main's own unit run stayed
green.

Verified locally: the test fails with 0.1.11.dev37977873285 and passes
with
0.1.13.dev38952644761; the native-proxy and types suites pass (88
tests).

The automation PR #8846 carries the same marin-iris-native bump together
with a dupekit bump and has been open since September; this PR is the
narrow fix so that unit (iris) passes on every branch now.

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[iac] Grant Marina IAP access to a registered principal (#10261)

Add an existing encrypted principal to `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor`
on the `marina` Cloud Run service, so they can reach marina.oa.dev. The
principal is already in the registry, so `iam_data.yaml` is unchanged.

A grant approver should run `review-grant` to confirm the decrypted
principal, then `pulumi up` on the `marin` stack.

Co-authored-by: Rafal Wojdyla <ravwojdyla@gmail.com>

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finelog] Increase forwarding throughput for dense log backlogs (#10238)

Increase regional Finelog → hub forwarding throughput so dense log
backlogs drain faster and delayed task logs reach Iris. Forward up to
four namespaces concurrently and read up to one million log rows per
read-and-send cycle. Requests retain their byte limit, and chunks remain
serial within the log namespace. The saved source cursor records
completed progress and cannot advance past a pending or retryable
request.

Encode each candidate chunk once. If its payload exceeds 150 MiB, split
it in half and process each half the same way. Process the left half
first to preserve source order. Source scans keep separate row-count and
segment bounds, and oversized single rows retain their existing
handling. Release the decoded Arrow batch before waiting for
acknowledgements. Slow-cycle diagnostics separate source reads, chunk
encoding, and RPC compression/transport/durable acknowledgement from
cursor persistence.

During the October 17 incident, RNO2A was roughly 395 million regional
sequence positions behind. Forwarding counters showed about 24,000
accepted positions/sec before deployment and 87,000–107,000/sec over
successive 71- and 65-second samples after deploying namespace
concurrency and larger reads. A dense source sample contained about
77,000 rows per second of event time; this measures production density.
Sequence positions can include gaps and filtered rows, so those counters
are not exact row counts. By 17:56 UTC, backlog was down to 91 positions
and all 417 rows for the affected task were present on the hub. The
chunk-splitting follow-up remains undeployed.

A local benchmark on one million synthetic NCCL-shaped rows with six log
columns and 294 MB of Arrow IPC output reduced serialization attempts
from seven to three compared with the deployed sizing search. Bytes
serialized, including discarded attempts, fell from 1,010 to 589 MB;
both versions produced two requests. With 100,000 narrow rows followed
by 100,000 wide rows, halving produced nine requests against eight with
the packing search. Halving accepts underfilled requests to avoid the
sizing search. These measurements describe serialization work; they do
not establish an end-to-end throughput improvement.

A bounded million-row regional read took 1.32 seconds initially and 0.19
seconds on repeat. Later live scans took 5.4–8.2 seconds in 12–16-second
cycles, including a 128-segment window returning only 424,000 rows. Read
cost varies with segment geometry and cache state. An isolated local
server capped at four CPUs acknowledged compressed 500,000-row writes in
0.70–0.78 seconds. Live hub samples showed about three active cores on a
four-core VM, compaction/index work, and near-zero disk I/O wait. The
largest resolved perf symbols involved copying, comparisons, and page
faults; stripped Rust symbols limited attribution. These probes do not
fully apportion live cycle time; the added stage timings expose the
remaining waits.

[Incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/780).

---------

Co-authored-by: rjpower <rjpower@users.noreply.github.com>
